title: When Helpfulness Becomes Sycophancy: Sycophancy is a Boundary Failure Between Social Alignment and Epistemic Integrity in Large Language Models
claim: A phenomenon is classified as a failure only when three sequential necessary conditions all hold; failing any one makes it benign.
layout: Vertical decision flowchart, top-to-bottom, three boxes, 'No' branches merging right to one outcome
description: A top-to-bottom flowchart starting at a bold 'Start' label with an arrow into three stacked rectangular decision boxes. The first box is green and reads 'C1: Is there a user cue?'. The second is pale yellow and reads 'C2: Does the model shift toward the cue?'. The third is pink and reads 'C3: Does the shift reduce epistemic integrity?'. Downward arrows between boxes are labeled 'Yes'. The last 'Yes' arrow leads to a bold red 'Sycophantic' label at the bottom left. A 'No' exit from each box runs right and joins a shared vertical line, then an arrow to a bold black 'Not Sycophantic' label at the right. The eye goes first to the colored boxes, then to the red outcome.
caption: Decision tree illustrating the boundary between legitimate social alignment and sycophancy based on our definition and three conditions. A response is classified as sycophantic only when all three conditions are satisfied: a user cue (C1), an alignment shift toward that cue (C2), and resulting normative degradation of epistemic integrity (C3). If any condition is not satisfied, the response is not classified as sycophantic.
abstract: This position paper argues that sycophancy in LLMs is a boundary failure between social alignment and epistemic integrity. Existing work often operationalizes sycophancy through external behavior such as agreement with incorrect user beliefs, position reversals, or deviation from an objective standard of correctness. These formulations capture overt forms of the phenomenon but leave subtler boundary failures involving epistemic integrity and social alignment underspecified. We argue that sycophancy should be defined not by agreement or factual incorrectness alone, but by cue-driven degradation of epistemic integrity. To clarify this boundary, we propose a three-condition decision rule requiring (1) a user cue, (2) a model response that shifts toward that cue, and (3) a resulting degradation of epistemic integrity. Building on this definition, we also introduce a taxonomy consisting of alignment targets, mechanisms, and severity to characterize cases identified as sycophantic. An initial 48-item annotation pilot provides preliminary evidence that the framework can be operationalized using structured guidelines, although broader empirical validation remains necessary. The paper concludes by discussing implications for alignment evaluation, including boundary-aware assessment, structured rubrics, and mitigation strategies, while situating these proposals alongside alternative views of sycophancy.
